title: Why the Workshop closed: economics and the need for arts education
summary: He blames economics, noting the group's earnings and the absence of mentors, and argues New Orleans needed jazz and arts education.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Advice to young musicians starting out

blocks.x: Can you address a little bit about what do you think the forces were that led to the closure? I mean, I know you said there were lots of other problems, but were there any other things that you think led to the closure?

Just economics. Had we been able to sustain ourselves as well? See, that was a period, as I said, where, say, from 64 up to that period, even for New Orleans, I mean, this was a period that we were making upward of, say, $350 to $500 a week per person and better sometimes, which is, many times musicians don't make, on a local level, they aren't doing it well here now in the 90s or late 80s that wasn't happening. The group was very popular. We were able to get some very good bookings, and we were recognized as being one of the best, if not the best, jazz group in New Orleans at that particular time. And all of our mentors were sort of doing other projects. I think Alvin had gone to start his program at Southern, so we weren't hearing much of him here. Ellis was off with his other projects, and the people that we had looked up to, for a while, we were carrying the torch of making sure that modern jazz or post-traditional jazz was going to survive and somehow forge ahead to make for a more progressive environment to wake up this community, wake up the educators to let them know that there was a vital need for jazz education, just music and arts education, to develop the kinds of things that were happening in New York and other key capitals of the world where they had these centers for the performing arts, where they had these things where up-and-coming painters, dancers, musicians, actors, and so forth, there were special facilities when you had all these gifted people in the schools that was always, generally the artists are thought of as being a little bit weird, a little bit different from your average student, or some people even thought of them as being aloof, where we knew that they had a very special talent and they were just misunderstood and not being guided and molded and shaped or given a facility and a technique so that they could really express this uniqueness that people call weird. and we knew that this was something that New Orleans had to wake up to and say, we got a lot of very special people here in many, many disciplines and we had better address that just as we addressed any other aspect of academics or athletics or something else that the arts were probably one of the most vibrant and one of the most vital things that we had to offer.
